10090-peaceless-europe:
Francesco S. Nitti's 1922 book argues that Europe, four years after the armistice, still has no peace. Its chapters treat Europe without peace and the peace treaties as a continuation of war. They cover the treaties' origin and aims, the conquerors and the conquered, and the indemnity from the defeated enemy with the anxieties of the victors.

A final chapter weighs Europe's post-war reconstruction and peace policy, and the author includes numerous secret official documents. Nitti, an Italian statesman, writes with insider knowledge. Readers get a sharp, early critique of Versailles, from a man who helped make the peace he questions.
1182-dope:
Sax Rohmer sends his detectives into London's opium underworld, where a drug ring run from Chinatown feeds the cravings of rich and poor alike. Inspector Kerry and his aide track the traffic from foggy docks to fashionable drawing rooms, while a mysterious eastern hand pulls the strings.

The tale is lurid pulp, full of dens, disguises, and narrow escapes, and it trades on the fears of its age about drugs and foreign crime. Rohmer writes at a brisk clip, and the mystery holds to the last page. The book suits readers of period thrillers, read with eyes open to its bias.
12309-love-affairs-of-the-courts-of-euro:
Thornton Hall published Love Affairs of the Courts of Europe, a book of royal romances, dedicated to his cousin Lenore. Hall, a barrister and author of love romances of the aristocracy, gathers scandalous and sentimental tales from palaces.

Chapters include a comedy queen, the Bonnie Prince bride, the peasant and the empress, a crown that failed, and a queen of hearts. A mid-book scene has Marie Mancini Colonna, dying in a good Samaritan house at Pisa, write her own epitaph with failing hand: Dust and Ashes. Hall writes for readers who liked history with love interest. The book is gossipy, romantic, and lightly sourced, a popular history of courts as bedrooms and thrones.
12590-the-shadow-of-the-rope:
E. W. Hornung's 1906 novel, The Shadow of the Rope, illustrated by Harvey T. Dunn, opens with the end of a life and the case for the crown. Chapters promise a man in a train, a man in the street, a peripatetic providence, a morning call, the dove and the serpent, and a slight discrepancy.

Rachel's champion, a battle royal, an Australian room, a chance encounter and the whole truth follow, through darkest hour to dawn. Hornung, creator of Raffles, writes a courtroom and mystery tale about a woman under suspicion and the rope that shadows her. The novel mixes trial drama with detection, in an Edwardian manner both tense and polite.
15576-a-system-of-instruction-in-the-pra:
This system of instruction in the practical use of the blowpipe appeared in New York, London, Paris, and Madrid in 1858. It offers a graduated course of analysis for students and all engaged in examining metallic combinations. It teaches a small, portable laboratory: flame, supports, and reagents, applied to ores and alloys.

Part one lists utensils in order: the blowpipe itself, oil and spirit lamps, charcoal and platinum supports, iron spoons, and glass tubes. Reagents follow, from carbonate of soda and borax to microcosmic salt, nitrate of cobalt, and test papers, with special reagents for harder cases. The course moves step by step from simple tests to full analysis. It shows nineteenth-century chemistry as a craft of hand, eye, and flame.
15992-come-rack-come-rope:
A historical novel by Robert Hugh Benson, author of By What Authority and The King's Achievement, issued in New York by P. J. Kenedy and Sons. Benson, a Catholic writer, sets his tale in Elizabethan England, when priests faced rack and rope. Robin rides to meet his love Marjorie on a still day of frost, under a sky arched like terrible crystal. His eyes should shine, but they do not.

Priest-hunters, hidden Masses, and martyrdom shadow the lovers' road. Benson writes with fire for the recusant cause, praising courage without hiding cost. The title itself is a defiance: come rack, come rope, faith will stand. The novel endures as a Catholic classic of persecution: love tested by terror, and truth kept at any price.
16442-the-doctrine-of-evolution-its-basi:
Henry Edward Crampton, a Columbia zoology professor, delivered these Hewitt Lectures in 1906 and 1907 and printed them in 1911. He lays out the case for evolution from animal structure, growth, and fossil remains, then treats it as a natural process. Later lectures carry the idea into human bodies, human minds, and social life.

The book closes with evolution and the higher human life, asking what the doctrine means for conduct and hope. Crampton writes for a general audience, with clear chapters and no heavy jargon. It gives a calm, early twentieth-century survey of a theory still hotly fought in public.
167-american-hand-book-of-the-daguerreot:
S. D. Humphrey's handbook gave American photographers the approved methods of their art. The American Hand Book of the Daguerreotype, in its fifth edition of 1858, covers preparing chemicals and combinations for heliographic impressions. Daguerreotype, electrotype, and related processes all appear.

Humphrey writes for practitioners, with recipes, cautions, and workshop detail rather than theory. Page marks in this electronic text follow the print original. The book shows photography as a hands-on trade in its first decades. Collectors and historians still consult it for period practice. Humphrey's fifth edition shows a craft maturing from novelty into a steady trade.
16926-skookum-chuck-fables-bits-of-histo:
Skookum Chuck wrote this 1915 Canadian book of fables and bits of history through the microscope, copyright Canada by R. D. Cumming, with some pieces first seen in the Ashcroft Journal. Fables run from a rolling stone and Cultus Johnny into a booby man and hard times Hance. A too sure man, an unloved man, and a chief bigger than he looked follow. Simple Simon up to date, a high class Eskimo, and sweet young things appear. A real Santa Claus and a retreat from Moscow close the fables. History bits take up Lycurgus, Joan of Arc, and voices long dead.

Skookum Chuck writes in a rough, humorous, frontier voice, with morals tucked in jokes. His fables mix British Columbia life with old history. Readers who like Canadian humor and tall tales will find a rare, local book, full of color and a microscope's eye for small truths.
17953-the-haunters-the-haunted-ghost-sto:
Ernest Rhys edited this 1921 London ghost book, The Haunters and the Haunted, gathering tales of the supernatural from books, local lore, and legend. Rhys thanks a long list of living writers, from Thomas Hardy to Arthur Machen, for leave to reprint their work.

The first part runs literary ghosts, led by Poe's Fall of the House of Usher, with tales of haunted houses, spectre brides, and a spectral coach. The second part turns to real places: Glamis Castle, Powys Castle, and Croglin Grange. It is a rich, old-style ghost shelf, made for winter nights and readers who love a good chill.
18854-the-gourmet-s-guide-to-europe:
Lieutenant-Colonel Newnham-Davis and Algernon Bastard wrote this gourmet's guide to Europe for Grant Richards of London in 1903, edited by Newnham-Davis. It opens in Paris, the culinary center, and moves through French provincial towns, Belgian towns, and Brussels before crossing the continent.

Chapters cover Holland, German towns, Berlin, Switzerland, Italy, Spain and Portugal, Austria and Hungary, Roumania, Scandinavia, Russia, Turkey, and Greece. Each chapter names restaurants with a past and restaurants of today, with notes on local food, wines, and supping places. The guide serves travelers who judge a city by its table as much as by its sights.
19654-alexander-pope:
Leslie Stephen wrote this life of Alexander Pope for the English Men of Letters series, edited by John Morley and published in London in the late eighteen hundreds. Stephen notes that no full life of Pope yet existed, despite a vast literature on his life and works.

The study is frank about Pope's faults, including letters to two sisters in which he professed himself their slave week by week. Stephen's short life remains a sharp, fair guide to the poet of the Rape of the Lock and the Essay on Man.
19983-recollections-of-europe:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote Recollections of Europe from his years abroad, 1826 to 1833. He grants it may seem late to describe the ordinary traits of Europe's peoples. Most people, he notes, judge other nations through reports alone. No two witnesses report the same country in the same way. His own account is what the book offers. Cooper lived in England, France, Switzerland, and Italy in those years.

Cooper was America's first writer to win fame across the Atlantic. His European books mix travel, politics, and national comparison. He judges monarchies and republics with a democrat's bias. The Recollections preserve an American eye on Europe after Napoleon. They also show fame's burdens abroad. Historians read them beside his novels with profit.
20926-the-register-of-ratlinghope:
A prior and twenty-nine canons held Ratlinghope at the Dissolution, yet its past stays dim. The Register of Ratlinghope notes its goods were worth five pounds, eleven shillings yearly. In May 1546 they were sold to Robert Longe, a London mercer.

Parish registers keep births, weddings, and burials across long runs of years. Shropshire's Ratlinghope, a wild hill parish, speaks here in bare lists. Names and dates that look dry hold whole lost lives in seed. Family and local historians mine such registers for kin, tenure, and the slow change of a place through plague, war, and peace.
21006-the-governments-of-europe:
Working accounts of how Europe's states run fill Frederic Austin Ogg's The Governments of Europe. His 1913 book treats western and central Europe as the systems then stood. Each land's form, he aims to show, must be seen as it works in fact.

Cabinets, parliaments, kings, and courts pass in clear, school-ready order. Ogg, a noted teacher of government, wrote for students who needed facts fast. His survey froze Europe's old order one year before it crashed in war. Readers can still use it to grasp the world the Great War swept away in four hard years.
21114-heroes-of-modern-europe:
Alice Birkhead's Heroes of Modern Europe, first published in London in 1913, tells European history through lives. Early chapters cover Dante, Lorenzo the Magnificent, and Savonarola, the prior of San Marco. Martin Luther, Emperor Charles V, and William the Silent follow as the story moves north.

Birkhead wrote other popular histories, including lives of Marie Antoinette and Peter the Great. Eight illustrations support the text, which opens with the fall of Rome and the coming of Teutonic invaders. The book offers young readers a parade of poets, rulers, and reformers, each standing for a turn in Europe's story from the Middle Ages onward.
21188-tom-swift-and-his-giant-telescope:
Victor Appleton's Tom Swift returns in this 1939 volume, published by Whitman of Racine, Wisconsin. Tom tells his chum Ned Newton that his new device should teach him more about the planets. The giant telescope is the latest project from the Swift works at Shopton.

Suspicions, an accident, and a murderous attempt follow in the chapter list. Tom is drugged, goes deep-sea diving, and is trapped by a sea monster before success arrives. The ten-chapter telling is shorter and punchier than the older Tom Swift books. It shows the young inventor series still running on invention, danger, and loyal friends.
21539-the-blue-envelope:
Roy J. Snell's The Blue Envelope, a 1922 adventure story for girls, opens with a disappearance in a horseshoe bay. Two girls fish for shrimps between rocky cliffs, one rowing, one lifting a wire net. Marian, the elder, was raised on the Alaskan tundra.

Marian hunted rabbits, ptarmigan, caribou, and white wolves with her father in her teens. She shoots as steady and sure as most boys her age. Chapters promise a visit to the Chukches, a dread white line, and a lonesome island. The blue envelope itself vanishes mid-tale, and its secret drives the hunt to the end.
21704-six-months-at-the-cape:
Letters home make up this travel book by R. M. Ballantyne, written to a friend he calls Periwinkle. Ballantyne had spent six years as a young clerk for the Hudson's Bay Company in Canada. That trip taught him to look closely at new lands and write down what he saw. Here he turns the same sharp eye on South Africa, at the Cape.

The letters describe the country, its towns, its people, and the daily life of a visitor far from home. Ballantyne later became famous for boys' adventure tales like The Coral Island. This book shows the working traveler behind those tales, gathering facts on the spot because readers had caught errors in his early work.
23364-a-reversion-to-type:
Josephine Daskam set this nineteen hundred three school story in a classroom where a tired teacher calls the roll. Girls chatter, bustle, and beg pardon with great politeness, while the teacher, worn out by the heat and the noise, longs for quiet.

Midway up the room sits a tall, dark girl, well dressed and oddly calm, who looks at her teacher with poise but seems far away in spirit. The story follows what that stillness hides: a pull back toward an older family cast of mind, at odds with school rules and town ways. Daskam writes the clash with care, asking how much of a girl is her own and how much is handed down.
26042-an-introduction-to-the-history-of-:
James Harvey Robinson, professor of history at Columbia, introduces the history of Western Europe in this Ginn volume of 1902 to 1903. Quoting Fustel de Coulanges that history is no easy science, since human society is infinitely complex. Robinson moves from Europe before the barbarian invasions through German invasions, the rise of the papacy, monks, Charles Martel, Pippin, and Charlemagne.

Later chapters take up feudalism, France, England in the Middle Ages, and Germany and Italy in the tenth and eleventh centuries. Luther's attack on the church resounds like a trumpet call, Robinson says, as German money drifts weightlessly over the Alps to Italy and comes back heavy as lead. The book is a clear, broad textbook for students of the West.
26204-a-letter-from-the-lord-bishop-of-l:
The Lord Bishop of London's letter to the clergy and people of London and Westminster answers two great shocks of earthquake. It was printed in 1750 by John Whiston in Fleet Street, at three pence. The bishop calls his people brethren and friends, and he warns that wickedness spreading through the great cities must give every serious Christian painful thoughts.

He reads the quakes as a summons from God to repentance, sent first to London and its neighbourhood, where the shaking was felt most. Thoughtless sinners, he says, may stay deaf, and little philosophers may rest on natural causes alone. Magistrates too must answer for power used or connived at. The letter blends pastoral care with stern warning, in the plain pulpit style of its age.
27316-that-gospel-sermon-on-the-blessed-:
D. L. Moody's That Gospel Sermon on the Blessed Hope is number sixteen in the series. It records a sermon delivered at the Great Chicago Tabernacle on January 5, 1877, and repeated at the Boston Tabernacle on April 29. Moody takes Second Timothy three sixteen: all scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine.

Some say prophecy should be let alone because the church does not agree. Moody argues that God would not have put prophecy in the Bible if he did not mean us to study it. The blessed hope is the return of the Lord, and believers must watch, ready at midnight like the five wise virgins, for the trump of God.
28697-down-the-slope:
James Otis wrote this 1899 boys' novel about life in a coal-mining town. Its hero is a breaker boy, one of the children who sorted coal above the mines. The story follows him through warnings, a shaft accident, a mob, a struggle, and a rescue. Later chapters bring a lawsuit over a mine title, amateur detectives, and a trial that ends in acquittal and victory.

The book mixes mine adventure with a courtroom plot, giving young readers both underground danger and a lesson in fair dealing. Otis, also the author of Toby Tyler, knew how to keep a chapter ending on a sharp edge. Down the Slope remains a vivid period story of child labor in the mines, told as adventure rather than protest, and ending with a new mine and a fresh start.
28935-captain-dieppe:
Anthony Hope wrote this novel, Captain Dieppe, copyright 1899 and published by Doubleday, Page in 1906. Hope, author of The Prisoner of Zenda and Rupert of Hentzau, follows a captain fresh from failed plans, with fifty francs in his pocket and a spare wardrobe packed in a knapsack. Recognition would be inconvenient and perhaps dangerous, yet he marches up a long steep hill in a stormy dusk, hoping for food and shelter.

The chapters move from the house on the bluff and the man by the stream to the lady in the garden, the inn in the village, and a rendezvous by the cross. A journey to Rome and the luck of the captain close the tale. Readers get a romantic adventure in Hope's gallant style, with a hero who keeps cheerfulness as a virtue a stoic would not disdain.
29285-the-migrations-of-an-american-boat:
Howard I. Chapelle wrote this study, paper 25 from the Museum of History and Technology, on the migrations of an American boat type: the sharpie. The New Haven sharpie, a flat-bottomed sailing skiff, was built for oyster fishing around the middle of the nineteenth century. Cheap to build, easy to handle, fast, and seaworthy, it spread quickly.

Chapelle traces the type to Chesapeake Bay and North Carolina, to other areas, and into double-ended forms and modern development. Later, its speed made it popular for racing and yachting. Readers get a precise maritime history, with models and figures, showing how a working fishing boat traveled down the coast and changed as it went.
29570-rope:
Holworthy Hall's 1922 novel, printed by Dodd, Mead and Company of New York, opens as Henry comes blithely home with a heavy suitcase and a kit-bag. His Aunt Mirabelle marches out like a grenadier to watch him approach, wearing the same expression she has worn for twenty years. Henry has altered, developed, and advanced, but Mirabelle has changed neither her clothes nor her convictions.

Hall writes a comedy of family wills: if Henry listens in silence he is called sulky, and if he disputes her he is called rude. The rope of the title binds kin by duty, habit, and love. Readers of light American fiction will enjoy a witty, well-observed tale of an aunt, a nephew, and a household at odds.
29667-adrift-on-the-pacific-a-boys-sic-s:
Edward S. Ellis, author of The Young Pioneers and Adrift in the Wilds, wrote this 1911 boys' story of the sea and its perils, printed by A. L. Burt Company of New York. It opens a few hours before the steamer Polynesia sails from San Francisco to Japan. Captain Strathmore, watching the bustle on deck, is approached by a nervous, well-dressed gentleman leading a little girl by the hand.

The stranger asks the captain to take a passenger to Tokio for him, and the honest, bluff old captain, though tender-hearted, must weigh the request. Peril, drift, and rescue follow on the Pacific. Young readers and fans of old boys' adventure will find a brisk, seafaring tale in the classic Ellis manner.
29827-the-life-and-amours-of-the-beautif:
Kate Percival, the Belle of the Delaware, tells her own life in this volume, printed in London and Paris in 1903. She opens with a bold claim: she will disguise nothing and conceal nothing, but relate all just as it happened. She calls herself a woman of pleasure who has drained its cup to the dregs, yet she promises to tell her most explicit scenes in decent language, without coarse words.

Her childhood chapter sets the scene in a small Pennsylvania village on the Delaware, about thirty miles from Philadelphia. Her father's house stood within yards of the river, backed by a high hill and flanked by dense woods. White sails passed on sunny days, while winter nights turned the river dark. The memoir that follows is frank, colorful, and written for adult readers of its day.
30715-where-there-s-hope:
Jerome Bixby writes Where There's Hope, illustrated by Kelly Freas, opening with a tagline that women had made up their minds and nothing could change them, yet something had to give. Mary Pornsen tells Hugh Farrel, chief medical officer of the Exodus Seven, that if he called her to have a child, he can forget it, since the girls have decided.

Farrel sighs, leans back, and asks Mary's husband Ralph how he feels. Ralph looks at Mary uncomfortably, starts to speak, then hesitates, and Farrel sighs again, closing his eyes. With all the boys, wives hold the whip hand, and argument brings a flat refusal: no sex at all, children or otherwise. Bixby turns a colony's birth strike into sharp social science fiction.
31307-one-purple-hope:
Henry Hasse's story, printed in Planet Stories in July 1952, follows Joel Latham, an Earthman of thirty, once a tall, upright spaceman roaming the galaxies freely, now a tsith-addict beachcomber at Venusport. He wakes face down in brackish mire at the swamp's edge near the compound, under a humming ionic field. Pallid gweels pause in their work to stare, and hammering nausea bends him double.

The magazine's headnote promises one last chance for a man who has lost everything to the drug. The illustration shows his resolve to face death on his own terms rather than drown in the mire. Bleak, vivid, and compassionate, the tale gives a ruined spaceman a final morning to choose how he will meet his end.
32175-preliminary-survey-of-a-paleocene-:
Robert W. Wilson's Preliminary Survey of a Paleocene Faunule from the Angels Peak Area, New Mexico, appeared in the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, on February 24, 1951. It forms volume five, number one, pages one to eleven, with one figure in the text. Wilson was one of the publication's editors, with E. Raymond Hall, A. Byron Leonard, and Edward H. Taylor. It was printed at Topeka through the state printer.

Wilson notes that David Baldwin, collecting for E. D. Cope, may have worked the area in the eighteen-eighties. The first published record of mammalian fossils from the Angels Peak badlands came from Walter Granger in 1917, after field work in the preceding summer. Granger's specimens were usually poorly preserved, though occasionally rather abundant locally. Readers get a short, preliminary scientific paper, surveying the Paleocene animal life of a New Mexico badlands area.
32346-keep-your-shape:
Robert Sheckley's tale, printed in Galaxy in November 1953, follows Pid the Pilot and his Grom crew toward a green planet. Third from its sun, it is the only life-bearing world in its system. Twenty earlier Grom expeditions set out to prepare the planet for invasion and vanished without a word. Pid, Ilg the Radioman, and Ger the Detector descend anyway, with compact Displacers stored in body pouches.

The Grom are elastic beings, and shape discipline matters to them: bodies that flow carelessly give away mood and intent. Pid reminds his crew to hold form as they face an innocent-looking world that has already swallowed twenty fleets. Sheckley builds humour and menace from that single rule of war, as a race built to bend meets a planet that will not break.
32551-big-stupe:
Charles V. De Vet's tale, printed in Galaxy in March 1955, follows Bruckner, a man deeply sure of his own worth, carried into a native ceremony by Sweets and Majesky. Bruckner, resting his broad beam on their joined arms, winks to share a joke about a necessary ritual, sure, like most thoroughly disliked men, that he is popular with the boys. Sweets, staggering under the weight, notes natives waiting across a red-sand plain.

The chief sits on a dais carried by eight followers, dressed in long streamers of many-coloured ribbons, with a ribbon rope for a diadem. Only Bruckner outshines him, in full regalia fit for a Gallic king of the second century, complete with a jewel-studded gold crown. De Vet's framing note warns that the natives handle clever outsiders better than outsiders handle them.
32557-an-humble-address-and-earnest-appe:
Josiah Tucker's Humble Address and Earnest Appeal, by a doctor of divinity, asks landed gentlemen in Great Britain and Ireland to judge a question. Would connection with, or separation from, the continental colonies of America best serve national advantage? Tucker addresses readers by their great interest in landed property, liberal education, elevated rank, and enlarged views, calling them ablest to judge and fittest to decide.

The tract argues, with the bluntness of a clergyman-economist, that Britain's interest may lie in letting colonies go rather than holding them by force and tax. Its author, though below his readers' notice by rank, presses a case about trade, empire, and the costs of rule. The appeal remains a key source for the American Revolution debate from the British side.
32953-quest-of-the-golden-ape:
Ivar Jorgensen and Adam Chase's serial, published across Amazing Stories in early 1957, follows a man who wakes with no past at all. He keeps only a dim memory of terror, a mother's cry for vengeance, and the slaughter of his own people. That broken memory drives him forward through a strange world of hidden cities, clocks, caverns, and distant ice fields.

Chapter by chapter the quest widens, from a mansion of mystery to the plains of Ofrid and the road to Nadia, as allies and captors cross his path. The tale mixes lost-world adventure with a search for identity, asking whether a man without a childhood can still claim a cause. It reads as fast, colorful pulp adventure, built for readers who wanted wonder at every turn.
33080-a-letter-from-mr-cibber-to-mr-pope:
Colley Cibber's Letter from Mr. Cibber to Mr. Pope, dated 1742, appears here in an Augustan Reprint Society edition with an introduction by Helene Koon. It was published by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library in 1973 as publication number 158. The letter belongs to one of the liveliest quarrels in English letters. The quarrel is between the actor-manager and poet laureate Cibber and the satirist Alexander Pope, who had made Cibber a butt in The Dunciad.

Koon's introduction sets the letter in that feud, where stage, poetry, and personal insult mixed. Cibber writes with the confidence of a man of the theater answering a poet's pen, and his prose shows why contemporaries found him both maddening and entertaining. For students of Pope, Cibber, and eighteenth-century literary war, this short reprint gives a primary voice in a famous dispute, with scholarly help for modern readers.
33481-the-guns-of-europe:
Joseph A. Altsheler's Guns of Europe, published in 1915, opens his World War series with a tale of young Americans caught in the Great War's first months. Altsheler, author of The Guns of Bull Run, writes of boys who meet war in Europe, with battles, escapes, and friendships that test their courage. Charles Wrenn's illustrations add to the adventure.

The novel's appeal lies in its brisk, boy-centered view of a vast war, told in plain, stirring prose. Its heroes learn war's cost as well as its thrill, and its scenes move from camps to front lines. For readers who enjoy historical adventure, The Guns of Europe offers a lively, old-fashioned start to a series on war's many fronts.
33552-acanthus-and-wild-grape:
F. O. Call's Acanthus and Wild Grape, copyrighted in Canada in 1920, gathers poems first published in Canadian magazines, from the University Magazine to the Canadian Bookman. Call, author of In a Belgian Garden, divides his book into Acanthus and Wild Grape, with poems like The Answer and Wild Grape itself. His verse speaks of nature, love, and Canadian life with a lyrical voice.

The collection suits readers who love early Canadian poetry, with a poet's eye for garden, vine, and season. Its tone is gentle and musical, best read slowly, poem by poem. For fans of Call, Acanthus and Wild Grape offers a charming, well-crafted volume, rooted in the magazines that first welcomed it.
33936-clever-hans-the-horse-of-mr-von-os:
Oskar Pfungst wrote this study of Clever Hans, the horse of Mr. von Osten, translated from the German by Carl L. Rahn and published in New York in 1911. A preface by James R. Angell and an introduction by Professor C. Stumpf frame the work, which bears on both animal and human psychology. Fifteen figures and one picture aid the text.

Pfungst tests how a horse that seemed to count and answer questions really read small, unconscious cues from people around him. The case stirred months of newspaper debate in Germany. The book remains a classic lesson in careful testing and in how easily belief outruns proof.
4015-the-hairy-ape:
Eugene O'Neill's play in eight scenes follows Yank, a stoker in a ship's engine room, who learns that the rich world above deck sees him as a beast. A visit below by a rich young woman named Mildred, in a white dress, shocks both of them and sets Yank searching for a place to belong.

Yank moves from the stokehold to Fifth Avenue, to a union hall, to the zoo, asking where a man built for labor fits in a machine age. O'Neill writes in rough, pounding speech, with scenes that shift like a dream. The play remains a raw, short classic about class, pride, and a worker's hunger to be more than a tool.
5101-lives-of-the-english-poets-prior-co:
Samuel Johnson's Lives, written when he was sixty-eight, pairs short biographies of English poets with criticism of their verse. The present volume covers four figures: Matthew Prior, William Congreve, Sir Richard Blackmore, and Alexander Pope, tracing each man's career, character, and reputation.

Johnson judges poems as well as lives, praising strong lines and exposing weak ones with famous bluntness. The Pope life, longest of the four, is especially valued for its first-hand detail. Readers interested in Augustan poetry will find here biography and criticism combined, in prose that is itself a model of clear English judgment.
5132-letters-to-sir-william-windham-and-:
Henry St John, Lord Bolingbroke, wrote the letters gathered here to two very different friends: Sir William Windham, a political ally, and Alexander Pope, the poet. The long letter to Windham, finished in the summer of 1717, defends Bolingbroke's political career and conduct during his years of power and exile.

The letters to Pope are more personal, mixing friendship, philosophy, and comment on the age. Together they show a statesman explaining himself in his own voice. They remain useful reading for anyone interested in early eighteenth-century politics, the art of the familiar letter, and Bolingbroke's restless mind.
5978-an-autobiography-of-anthony-trollop:
Anthony Trollope wrote this memoir to appear after his death, leaving its publication to his editor's discretion. It traces his education from 1815 to 1834, his mother, and his long service in the General Post Office, then follows his first novels in Ireland and his slow climb to success.

Later chapters name Barchester Towers, Doctor Thorne, Framley Parsonage, and The Last Chronicle of Barset, with essays on novels, on English novelists, and on criticism. Trollope also covers magazines, copyright talks with America, and a run for Beverley. The book reads as a working writer's plain account of his craft.
6369-medieval-europe:
H. W. C. Davis, fellow and tutor of Balliol College, Oxford, writes Medieval Europe for the Home University Library, edited by Fisher, Murray, Thomson, and Brewster. His introduction warns that all divisions of history into periods are artificial in proportion as they are precise, for no event has a true beginning or end. Each age is a child of the past and parent of the future, transforming by imperceptible degrees.

Chapters run from the fall of Rome and barbarian kingdoms through empire, feudalism, papacy before Gregory VII, and the Hildebrandine church, to the medieval state, crusades, and free towns. Maps of barbarian kingdoms, France, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Alps support the text. Davis writes a short, clear survey, where kings, bishops, and towns share the stage and the Middle Ages emerge as transition, not darkness.
6733-memoir-of-father-vincent-de-paul-re:
A. M. Pope translates from French a memoir of Father Vincent de Paul, a religious of La Trappe, with a preface by Bishop Cameron of Arichat. The preface opens with Emperor Maximilian's reply to a courtier seeking a title for gold: wealth can be given, but only virtue can ennoble. True grandeur, it says, is the child of virtue alone.

Father Vincent's life, as told here, shows that virtue in monastic silence, prayer, and humble service. The memoir is devout and earnest, aimed at readers who seek a holy example. Memoir of Father Vincent de Paul is a quiet, pious life of a Trappist monk, told with reverence.
7322-our-hundred-days-in-europe:
Oliver Wendell Holmes outlines a summer excursion in Our Hundred Days in Europe, dedicating the book to his daughter Amelia, Mrs Turner Sargent, his faithful and devoted companion. The voyage leads to Liverpool, Chester, London, and Epsom, then on through Windsor, the Isle of Wight, Cambridge, Oxford, York, and Edinburgh. Stratford-on-Avon, Great Malvern, Tewkesbury, Bath, Salisbury, and Stonehenge follow.

Holmes writes as an elderly American man of letters revisiting old scenes with humour and affection, noting people as much as places. A portrait of Holmes at eighty-two fronts the volume. The book reads as a gentle farewell tour, full of talk, memory, and good company.
7405-the-real-dope:
Ring Lardner writes the First World War in the voice of an ordinary American soldier writing home to his friend Al. The letters begin on shipboard, on January 15, as the troops cross the Atlantic. The writer cannot say when they left or from where, since a German spy might pass the news to submarines, and that rule itself becomes part of the joke.

Lardner's soldier spells badly, brags gently, and notices everything: the food, the boredom, the officers, and the strangeness of France. The humor comes from the gap between the grand language of war and one man's plain, funny account of it. Illustrated and told entirely in letters, the book is a comic classic of the American doughboy abroad.
8493-the-last-hope:
Henry Seton Merriman's novel The Last Hope opens with a voice asking what the singer knows, and the answer, a hidden hope. Contents move from Le Roi Est Mort and Vive Le Roi through the return of the last hope. They continue with the marquis's creed, a dyke, castaways, a little boy who was a king, a mistake, an Italian house, and the secret of Gemosac.

Merriman, a popular adventure novelist, writes of exiled royalty and secret causes, in the romantic style of his day. Readers get a tale of legitimist plots and hidden heirs, with France and its exiles at the center. The novel's charm lies in its old-fashioned adventure, where hope itself becomes a character, hidden and pursued.
886-letters-from-the-cape:
Lady Duff Gordon wrote these letters from the Cape of Good Hope, edited by John Purves for a 1921 edition. Ill and seeking a warmer climate, she travelled to South Africa and wrote home about the land, its peoples, and its ways, with the candour and wit that made her letters famous.

The letters mix travel, health, and social observation, describing farms, towns, and the mixed society of the Cape. Purves's foreword notes they are less familiar than her Egyptian letters, yet just as vivid. The book gives readers a Victorian lady's view of South Africa, sharp, humane, and free of cant.
8898-cliff-castles-and-cave-dwellings-of:
S. Baring-Gould surveys cliff castles and cave dwellings across Europe, opening with a cliff-castle at Brengues. The Bishop of Cahors took refuge from the English, refused to submit, died there in 1367, and saw the castle captured by the English in 1377. A Cymbeline epigraph, the house in the rock, no life to ours, sets the theme. Chapter one treats prehistoric cave-dwellers: chalk and dolomitic limestone, where first men lived, their Eden in chalk lands, migration, pit dwellings, and troglodytes.

Les Eyzies, the Hotel du Paradis, the first colonists of the Vezere valley, and their painting and sculpture follow, with rock dwellings in Champagne and beyond. Baring-Gould, antiquary and novelist, combines geology, archaeology, and travel with a storyteller's flair. Readers interested in how humans have lived in rock, from caves to castles, will find a richly illustrated tour of Europe's most dramatic homes.
8942-the-last-hope:
Henry Seton Merriman writes The Last Hope as a romance of legitimist intrigue, opening with chapters called Le Roi est Mort, Vive le Roi. The Return of the Last Hope. A hidden hope answers a crying voice in the epigraph. The contents follow the marquis's creed, a dyke, castaways, a scent, and the little boy who was a king. A mistake, an Italian house, a beginning, the secret of Gemosac, within the gates. The lifted veil carry the middle, before the turn of the tide, gamblers, the Pont Royal, and the city that soon forgets.

In the breach, Nineteen, and number eight Ruelle St Jacob close the list shown, as a lost Bourbon heir and his supporters gamble everything on restoration. Merriman blends French history, conspiracy, and romance with his usual brisk plotting. Readers who enjoy historical adventure with a royalist flavour will find a stirring tale.
9653-a-wreath-of-virginia-bay-leaves-poe:
Janey Hope Marr edited A Wreath of Virginia Bay Leaves, poems of her father James Barron Hope, Virginia's laureate. Marr dedicated the book to her son Barron Hope Marr, who bore his grandfather's name and image. Her introduction claims Hope fired the fancy with concrete images, not vague abstractions. His kin had served Virginia since the Revolution, when James Barron the elder built its colonial navy.

Poems inside include summer studies and the Washington Memorial Ode, with odes and lyrics of Southern pride. Hope's verse favors noble images and lofty thought. A reader gets a daughter's loving portrait of a Southern poet, and a wreath of verse for Virginia's past.
a-system-of-instruction-in-the-practical: This anonymous system of instruction teaches the practical use of the blowpipe in a graduated course of analysis, published in 1858 at New York, London, Paris, and Madrid. It is written for students and all those engaged in examining metallic combinations. It moves from the blowpipe itself through oil and spirit lamps, charcoal and platinum supports, iron spoons, and glass tubes. Reagents follow, from carbonate of soda and hydrate of baryta to bi-sulphate and oxalate of potassa.
a-wreath-of-virginia-bay-leaves-poems-of: James Barron Hope's poems gather into a wreath of Virginia bay leaves, edited by Janey Hope Marr. The volume is dedicated to the memory of Barron Hope Marr, the little lad who carried his grandfather's name and likeness. The introduction claims Hope as Virginia's laureate, a poet who fired imagination purely through noble odes, a living series of concrete images and pictures. His elder namesake organized the Virginia Colonial Navy in the Revolution, and his sons served gallantly.
alexander-pope: Leslie Stephen, in John Morley's English Men of Letters series, writes a compact life of Alexander Pope, the Augustan poet of satire and verse. Stephen weighs Pope's genius against his frailties, tracing his friendships, quarrels, and mastery of the heroic couplet. The study is frank and readable, giving a clear portrait of a poet whose wit and craft shaped English letters.
american-hand-book-of-the-daguerreotype:
S. D. Humphrey wrote this practical manual on the daguerreotype, the first widely used form of photography. The title page of this fifth edition is dated New York, 1858, and promises the most approved and convenient methods for preparing the chemicals and combinations used in the art. Humphrey's preface says working photographers had long wanted one concise, reliable handbook.

The chapters give working recipes and procedures. They cover coating and polishing plates, mixing chemicals, using the camera, and developing the image. The related electrotype process and other ways of taking pictures by light are included too. It is a trade manual, not a history, written for portrait studios at the height of the daguerreotype trade. For modern readers it preserves the exact bench practice of early photography.
an-autobiography-of-anthony-trollope:
An Autobiography, by Anthony Trollope, tells the most successful English novelist of his age how he did it. Trollope's contents begin with his education from 1815 to 1834 and a chapter on his mother, the writer Frances Trollope. Then comes the General Post Office, which employed him from 1834, and Ireland, where his first two novels were written in the 1840s while he rode his postal rounds.

Success arrives chapter by chapter: Barchester Towers and The Three Clerks, Doctor Thorne, the Cornhill Magazine and Framley Parsonage, Orley Farm, The Small House at Allington. Trollope pauses for three famous chapters on novels and the art of writing them, on living English novelists, and on criticism itself. He counts his earnings, defends his daily page quota, and treats authorship as honest trade work. No Victorian writer left a plainer account of the business of books.
britannica-1911-baini-giuseppe:
Baini, Giuseppe (1775-1844), was an Italian priest and church composer. He was born at Rome in 1775. His uncle Lorenzo taught him composition first. Jannaconi taught him afterwards. His fine bass voice won him a chapel place in 1802.

In 1814 Baini became musical director of the pontifical choir. Few of his works were ever published. They showed the severe church style well. His ten-part Miserere dates from 1821. Pius VII ordered it for Holy Week. It still holds a place in Sistine Chapel services. Baini ranked higher as critic and historian. His Life of Palestrina appeared in 1828. It counts among the best works of its kind. The phrase Prince of Music for Palestrina starts with that book.
britannica-1911-brunck-richard-francois-:
Richard Francois Philippe Brunck (1729–1803) was a French classical scholar born at Strassburg on 30 December 1729. Educated at the Jesuits' College at Paris, he served in the Seven Years' War as a military commissary. At thirty he returned to his native town and resumed his studies, giving special attention to Greek, and he spent considerable sums publishing editions of the Greek classics.

His first edited work, the Anthologia Graeca of 1772 to 1776, startled European scholars: wherever an obscure passage could be made clear by altering the text. He altered it, whether manuscripts supported the new reading or not. Editions of Anacreon, Greek tragedians, Apollonius Rhodius, Aristophanes with a fine Latin translation, and Sophocles followed. The Sophocles of 1786, his best work, won him a royal pension of 2000 francs. Editions of Virgil and other Latin authors round out the list the entry gives.
britannica-1911-caripe:
Caripe is a small town of Venezuela, in South America. It stands in the state of Bermúdez. It lies about 53 miles east-south-east of Cumaná. Its population is only 580, the entry says. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its famous cave. Caripe is the chief station of the Capuchin missions. Those missions serve the Chayma Indians of the district. They were founded late in the 17th century.

The town stands 2635 feet above sea-level. It sits in a fertile valley of the Sierra Bergantín. The valley is long famed for its cool, healthy climate. Limestone caves near the town are its greater wonder. Humboldt described them in his Personal Narrative. The chief cave, the Cueva del Guácharo, runs 2800 feet inward. Night-hawks called guacharos nest in its dark recesses. Their young are killed in numbers for their oil.
britannica-1911-cope:
A cope is a church vestment of the Western Church. The word was once the same as cape and cap in root and use. Until fairly modern times it named an outdoor cloak for clergy and lay folk alike. The Latin name pluviale, or rain-cloak, tells the same tale. Both words show the garment's plain start in daily dress.

The shape keeps that start in plain view. Spread out, a cope forms near a full half-circle. A broad band runs along its straight edge. At the neck hangs a hood, a last trace of the old cloak. Rich growth turned a plain wrap into a robe of state. The long entry traces that growth through the ages. It ends with rules for its use in the English church. A canon of 1603 called for a decent cope in set services.
britannica-1911-giusti-giuseppe:
Giuseppe Giusti (1809-1850) was a Tuscan satirical poet, born at Monsummano on 12 May 1809. The 1911 Britannica entry describes a rich, cultivated father who taught the boy early, then placed him under a severe priest. Schooled at Florence, Pistoia and Lucca, Giusti wrote his first verses in those years.

In 1826 he went to Pisa to study law, disliked it, and took eight years over a four-year course. He lived gaily on short funds, the entry says, and learned the world at first hand. What he saw of society's vices and the folly of laws and customs, he later turned to account in his satire. The article follows his turn to earnest patriotic writing from 1832, with poems such as La Ghigliottina, and weighs the satires that made his name in Italy.
britannica-1911-kaleidoscope:
The kaleidoscope, its name built from Greek words for beautiful, form, and to view, is an optical toy that makes balanced patterns by reflection. Two mirrors set at an angle that divides the full circle evenly throw back repeated images in matching order. Sir David Brewster gave the device its present form about 1815, and it became popular at once for the beauty and range of its figures.

A like device by R. Bradley a hundred years earlier had sunk into neglect. In its simplest form the toy is a tube about twelve inches long. Two glass plates run its length at an angle of 60 degrees. One end carries a metal plate with a small hole for the eye, and the other a plate of muffed glass with a clear plate fixed by it. Designers have made much use of the instrument.
britannica-1911-la-farina-giuseppe:
Giuseppe La Farina (1815–1863) was an Italian author and politician, born at Messina. For his part in the rising of 1837 he had to leave Sicily. Back in 1839 he ran liberal newspapers until they were shut down, then moved to Florence. There he wrote works on the monuments of Germany, Italy and China, and a history of Italy in seven volumes (1846–1854). In 1847 he founded the democratic journal L'Alba, for Italian freedom and unity.

When Sicily rose in 1848 La Farina went home, sat as a deputy, and became minister of public instruction, then of war and marine. After a hard campaign against the Bourbon troops he was driven into exile in France in 1849. He settled at Turin in 1854 and in 1856 founded the Piccolo Corriere d'Italia. He presided over the Società Nazionale Italiana and, with Daniele Manin, urged the unity of Italy under Victor Emmanuel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agape:
Agape begins from funeral feasts honouring the dead, a practice reaching back almost to worship's beginnings. The dead beyond the tomb were thought to gain pleasure and advantage from offerings, which explains funeral furniture for their use. Arms, vessels, and clothes, not subject to decay, needed no renewal, but food did, hence feasts at set seasons. Yet the departed gained no relief from offerings to his shade unless accompanied by obligatory rites.

Nor was the funeral feast mere commemoration, since it was a true communion, with guests' food really meant for the departed. Milk and wine were poured on the earth around the tomb, while solid food passed through a hole in the tomb to the corpse. The practice was almost universal in the Graeco-Roman world. The entry then relates the agape to the Last Supper and the Eucharist, and cites Batiffol, Funk, Keating, and Leclercq.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-pop:
Alexander Pope was an English poet, born in London in May 1688 and dead at Twickenham in May 1744. Both his parents were Catholics, and he lived and died in the faith of his birth. His father, a linen merchant in Lombard Street, retired on a moderate fortune to Kensington, then Binfield, then Chiswick. He died there in 1717, after which Pope moved with his mother.

In November 1713 Pope issued proposals for a subscription translation of Homer's Iliad into English verse, the work that turned his fortunes. Later he fell deeply under the influence of Bolingbroke, and with the Dunciad of 1743 his literary activity ceased, though he tried to gather his works for an authoritative edition. No writer ever made more enemies, the entry says: Pope lashed Bufo, Sporus, Sappho, Atosa, and scores of others by name or thin disguise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antipope:
An antipope is a rival claimant to the Holy See, opposing a canonically elected pope. Unlawful pretenders recur through Church history, often exercising papal functions against the true holder. Hergenröther counts thirty.

Hippolytus, third century, Novatian in 251, Felix II in 355-365, Ursicinus in 366-367, Eulalius in 418-419, and Laurentius in 498-501. Constantine II in 767, Philip, eighth century, and Anastasius in 855. Leo VIII in 956-963, Boniface VII in 974, John XVI, tenth century, Gregory in 1012, and Sylvester III in 1044. Benedict X in 1058, Honorius II in 1061-72, and Guibert, or Clement III, in 1080-1100. Theodoric in 1100, Aleric in 1102, Maginulf in 1105, and Burdin, called Gregory VIII, in 1118. Anacletus II in 1130-38, Victor IV in 1159-64, Pascal III in 1164-68, Calixtus III in 1168-77, Innocent III in 1178-80, and Nicholas V in 1328-30. Robert of Geneva, Clement VII, 20 September 1378 to 16 September 1394, and Amadeus of Savoy, Felix V, November 1439 to April 1449. See also Dioscorus (died 530) and John XXIII (1370-1419), not the twentieth-century pope of that name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cope:
Herbert Thurston's entry defines the cope, Latin pluviale or cappa, as a long liturgical mantle, open in front and fastened at the breast with a band or clasp. Surviving monuments, pictures, and early copes alike show remarkably little change in the vestment from earliest ages. It differed from the earlier chasuble form only in this: the chasuble's straight edges were sewn together in front, the cope's left open.

The most conspicuous change over the past thousand years and more lies in hood shape, a feature in no way essential. History traces the earliest mention of a cappa to Gregory of Tours and the Miracula of Saint Martin. Meanwhile the old cappa nigra, or cappa choralis, a black choir cope, open or partly open in front and commonly hooded, continued in use. Under all these forms the cope has not substantially changed its character or shape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eastern-vicar:
In 1847 the Cape vicariate divided into Eastern and Western halves, and the Eastern half became its own vicariate. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how the Eastern vicariate was later cut three times more. As it stands, it runs from the Orange River in the north to the Indian Ocean in the south. It is bounded west by a chain of civil districts and east by Tembuland, Griqualand East, and Basutoland.

On 27 December 1847 Doctor Devereux was consecrated at Cape Town as bishop of Paneas and first vicar apostolic, by Doctor Griffith, under whom he had worked nine years. A gift through the Dhanis family of Belgium aided the new mission. The entry counts thirty-seven men religious and three hundred and thirty-one women religious, serving more than thirteen thousand Catholics, few of them natives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-europe:
Europe is treated here in a long survey article that moves from the land itself to the faith of its peoples. It opens with the name, traced to Aegean sailors who used Semitic words for sunset and sunrise for lands west and east of their sea. It then maps the continent's bounds, from North Cape to Cape Tarifa, and measures its length, breadth, and area. 

The second half turns to people and religion. It covers population, political divisions, and the spread of Christianity from its early centuries through the Crusades, the Reformation, and the Counter-Reformation. It closes with the present state of religion country by country, how each state treats its churches, and full tables of religious statistics drawn from censuses around 1900. The result is a snapshot of a continent on the eve of modern change.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-vi-an:
When Pope Sergius IV died in June 1012, a rival claimant known only as Gregory challenged the election of Benedict VIII and had himself made pope by a small faction. The entry follows this brief claimant from his hurried elevation to his swift expulsion from Rome.

Driven out, Gregory crossed to Germany and asked King Henry II for backing in December 1012. Henry promised a hearing under canon law and Roman custom, yet stripped him of the papal insignia and told him to stop acting as pope. After that rebuke, the record says, history hears nothing more of him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-viii-:
Mauritius Burdinus, a Frenchman born probably at Limoges, rose through Cluny and the Spanish church to become Archbishop of Braga before his career broke on imperial politics. Suspended by Paschal II after a quarrel with the primate, he went to Rome, won the pope's trust, and was sent to deal with Emperor Henry V in 1117.

On that mission Burdinus changed sides, crowned Henry at Easter, and was excommunicated. Months later Henry had a bribed Roman assembly proclaim him pope under the name Gregory, on 8 March 1118. Repeated excommunications followed, and Callistus II finally held him prisoner in monasteries until his death about 1137.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guadeloupe:
Basse-Terre's diocese gathers Guadeloupe with Les Saintes, Marie-Galante, La Désirade, and the French parts of St. Martin and St. Bartholomew in the West Indies. Columbus reached the main island in November 1493 and named it for Spain's Madonna of Guadalupe, and the island stayed French from 1653 apart from short English occupations.

After years under a prefect apostolic, reform of the colonial clergy led to a bull of September 1850 creating the bishopric as suffragan of Bordeaux. Its first bishop, the famed preacher Lacarrière, served from 1851 to 1853, and by 1905 the diocese counted 182,112 people, 37 parishes, and 54 priests beside its bishop and vicars-general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hope:
Hope, in its widest sense, is desire for something joined with expectation of obtaining it. Scholastics call it a movement of appetite toward a future good, hard to attain yet possible. This article limits itself to hope as a factor in the supernatural order, where it is defined as a divine virtue.

By that virtue, Christians confidently expect, with God's help, to reach eternal felicity and to have the means of securing it. Hope counts as divine not only because its object is God, but because of its special origin. It is an infused virtue, not the product of repeated acts or personal industry. Like faith and charity, God implants it directly in the soul, lifting a faculty beyond created limits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-sharpe:
James Sharpe, alias Pollard, born at York in 1577 and dead at Lincoln in 1630, was converted young and studied for priesthood at Valladolid's English College. Ordained in 1604, he returned to England in 1606. A singular trial awaited him there. Believing he must help his parents toward the faith, he visited them at Everingham. He was insidiously kept prisoner at home.

At home, disputations and entreaties alternated with threats, violence, and constant surveillance. His mother begged him on her knees to yield. His father asked authorities to keep him close at home in England rather than exile him. His constancy prevailed. Taken eventually to the archbishop's prison, then deported, he had entered the Society of Jesus in 1608 and became a noted missioner, constancy under family pressure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-francois:
Jean-François La Harpe, a French critic and poet born in Paris in 1739 and dead in 1803. He lost his father at ten, was raised by Sisters of Charity, and studied free at Collège d'Harcourt. Satirical verses landed him in Fort-l'Évêque prison, yet at twenty he published his Heroïdes and won fame with the tragedy Warwick.

La Harpe clung so close to Voltaire that wits called him Voltaire's monkey, though later tragedies failed. At the Mercure from 1768 he wrote notable criticism, won three Academy prizes in a row for praises of Henry IV, Fénelon, and Racine, and entered the Academy in 1776. His banned play Mélanie attacked religious vows and was widely read despite its tedium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-trappe:
La Trappe is the famed abbey of the Reformed Cistercians, set in a lonely forest valley with lakes and streams, eighty-four miles from Paris and nine from Mortagne in Normandy. Rotrou II, Count of Perche, built a chapel there in 1122 to fulfil a vow, then a monastery, raised to an abbey in 1140.

With Savigny, it joined Citeaux in 1147 under Clairvaux. Obscure for centuries, it suffered English raids in the fifteenth century and commendatory abbots in the sixteenth, leaving only mournful ruins. Renewal came with Abbot de Rance, who restored Citeaux's strict traditions and made La Trappe famed across Christendom. Suppressed in 1790, it was bought back by Dom Augustin de Lestrange in 1815 and lived again.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lippe:
Lippe was a small German principality of about 469 square miles, tucked between Westphalia and Hanover, with Detmold as its chief town. Its lords became counts of the empire in 1529, and the land won full independence as a principality in 1807, later joining the German Empire in 1871.

Faith shaped its story more than size did. Lutheran teaching took hold in Lemgo despite the ruler's efforts to stop it, and Calvinist teaching won out across most of the land after 1605, while Lemgo alone stayed Lutheran. Catholics stayed a small share, about 3.8 percent by 1905, and only in 1854 did an edict put the Catholic Church on equal legal footing with the state Calvinist church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-aube:
Philippe Aubert de Gaspé was a French Canadian writer, born at Quebec in 1786 to a family ennobled by Louis XIV in 1693. His grandfather fought under Montcalm at Carillon. Schooled at Quebec Seminary, he practised law briefly, served as sheriff, and, forced by misfortune to retire to Saint-Jean-Port-Joli on the St. Lawrence, spent thirty years in study there.

At seventy-five he produced Les Anciens Canadiens in 1861, a historical novel almost wholly based on fact and now a household word across Canada. It weaves his own chequered life into the fall of New France and the change of regime, whose eyewitnesses he had personally known. His Mémoires of 1866 continue and amplify its precious notes, a fine specimen of anecdotal history from a man whose experience spanned a century from the Conquest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protopope:
A protopope is a senior priest in the Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic churches. He roughly matches the Western archpriest or dean. This encyclopedia entry explains that the titles archpriest, protopriest and protopope generally mark the same rank. At times they were kept apart. The rank is the highest priest in his order, standing just below the bishop. By the fifth century the archpriest headed the college of priests and acted as the bishop's deputy.

Duties shifted with time and place, but the pattern holds. The protopope visited parishes and judged cases for the bishop. He stood in for the bishop in absence, or when the see fell vacant. The entry draws on Greek service books and church-law writers. Goar's Euchologion and modern studies of the Eastern churches both appear. Readers comparing Eastern and Western church order will find the parallels set out plainly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ruspe:
Ruspe is a titular see of Byzacena in Africa, mentioned only by Ptolemy and the Peutinger Table. Ptolemy places it on the coast between Acholla and Usilla; the Table puts it six, doubtless twenty-six, miles from Usilla. Scholars match it with Ksour Siad's ruins, seventeen miles from Acholla. Others put it at Henshir Sbia, four miles west of Cape Kapoudia, with its name living on at Koudiat Rosfa near Ras el Louza. Koudiat Rospa is more likely itself ancient Ruspe.

Four bishops of the see are known. Stephanus was exiled by King Huneric in 484. St Fulgentius was consecrated in 508 and died in 533. Felicianus, his companion in exile and successor, assisted at the Council of Carthage about 534. Julianus signed in 641 the Anti-Monothelite letter of Byzacena's bishops to Emperor Constantine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schaumburg-li:
Schaumburg-Lippe, a German principality ringed by Westphalia, Hanover, and a Hessian exclave, covers about 131 square miles with 46,650 people in 1910. Smallest German state by population, it is larger in area than Reuss-Greiz, Lübeck, and Bremen. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia counts a largely Lutheran land with a Catholic minority.

In 1905, of 44,992 people, 43,888 were Lutherans, 653 Catholics, and 246 Jews, leaving Catholics at about one and a half per cent. The principality grew from the old county of Schaumburg, also called Schauenburg, on the middle Weser, given as a fief by Emperor Conrad II to Adolph of Santersleben. Adolph built Schaumburg castle on the Nettelberg, and his heirs later gained Holstein and Schleswig as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shrine-of-gua:
Guadalupe is strictly the name of a picture, but the name spread to the church holding it and the town that grew around it. The place, called Guadalupe Hidalgo since 1822, stands three miles northeast of Mexico City. Pilgrimages have flowed there almost without break since 1531 and 1532. In the latter year a shrine rose at the foot of Tepeyac Hill and served for ninety years, still forming part of the parish sacristy.

A rich shrine followed in 1622 and a richer one in 1709. A parish church, a Capuchin convent, a well chapel, and a hill chapel were added in the 1700s. About 1750 the shrine became collegiate, it was joined to Saint John Lateran in 1754, and in 1904 it was made a basilica. The picture itself makes the shrine, taken as the Immaculate Conception, the woman with sun, moon, stars, and a supporting angel. Its interior renewal in Byzantine style retells that history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sinope:
Sinope, a titular see in Asia Minor suffragan to Amasea in Helenopontus, was a Greek colony on a Paphlagonian peninsula of very early origin. Some credit its founding to the Argonaut Autolycus. A Milesian colony was retaken by Greeks in 632 BC. Henceforth Sinope prospered greatly, founding colonies including Cerasus, Cotyora, and Trapezus, backing Athens in the Peloponnesian War, and sheltering Xenophon's Ten Thousand on their retreat.

Fruitlessly besieged in 220 BC by Mithridates IV, it was taken by Pharnaces in 183 BC and became the Pontic kings' capital and residence. It was the birthplace of Mithridates the Great. Lucullus captured it and restored its autonomy, and Caesar set up a colony there in 45 BC. Diogenes the Cynic and Aquila, translator of the Old Testament into Greek, were born there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-suppression-o:
Suppression of monasteries in Europe covers only religious houses dissolved since the Reformation, whether monastic or mendicant, and this entry treats Germany, the Iberian Peninsula, and Italy. English dissolutions have their own article, French ones belong under France, and the economics of Church landholding appear under Mortmain. The story opens with Westphalia in 1648, when Protestant princes gained over a hundred monasteries.

A second wave rose in the Catholic German lands near the middle of the eighteenth century. Called Josephinism, after Joseph II, it made the Church serve the State. Abbeys might stand only if they proved material use. Frederick II of Prussia pushed a general secularization plan, winning England and France, against Maria Theresa's opposition. Iberian and Italian dissolutions, and the precarious survival of orders under mere liberty guarantees, complete the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-pope:
Bishop of Rome, chief pastor of the whole Church, and Vicar of Christ on earth: that is the pope as this entry presents him. Latin papa, from Greek papas for father, once ranged widely as a title before settling solely on Rome's bishop, successor of Saint Peter. Other dignities cluster around the office: archbishop of the Roman province, primate of Italy and nearby islands, and sole patriarch of the Western Church.

Vatican Council's Pastor Aeternus declared the doctrine in four chapters: Peter's headship, its perpetuity in Roman pontiffs, jurisdiction over the faithful, and supreme power to define faith and morals. Election, powers, history, and titles follow in a long survey of an office that shaped a millennium of Christian life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trope:
A collective name, in liturgical hymnology, for texts of great variety written to amplify and embellish a complete liturgical text. Tropes attach closely to parts of the Mass or Office sung by the choir. Examples are the Introit, Kyrie, Gloria and Gradual, and they do not change the essential character of the original.

The most accurate definition calls a trope an interpolation in a liturgical text, or the embellishment made by interpolation, through introductions, insertions or additions. It differs from the Sequence, which is inserted between chants rather than woven into one. The entry gives examples from the Sanctus and the Christmas Introit to show the form at work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-rob:
Robert Thorpe was a Yorkshire priest executed at York in May 1591. He reached Reims in March 1584, was ordained deacon that December and priest in April 1585, and was sent to England a month later to labour in Yorkshire. He was arrested in bed very early on Palm Sunday at the house of his fellow martyr Thomas Watkinson at Menthorpe.

Someone saw palms being gathered the night before and told the nearest justice. Both men, naturally timid, met death with great fortitude. Thorpe, sentenced as a traitor for the sole reason that he was a priest, was hanged, drawn, and quartered. Watkinson, condemned as a felon for harbouring priests, was only hanged, having been offered his life if he would go to church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-western-vicar:
The Western Vicariate of the Cape of Good Hope, with the Central Prefecture, though different in name, is virtually one jurisdiction. From 1874 to 1882 the Central Prefecture lay under Lyons's Missionary Fathers; on their withdrawal part became the Orange River Prefecture under Salesian Oblates. The rest joined the Western Vicariate, now covering 82,757 square miles bounded by the Olifants River, Roggeveldt Mountains, Gouritz River, and the sea, including St Helena and Ascension.

In 1486 Bartolomeu Dias raised a cross on South African soil at Croix Island in Algoa Bay. The Cape became a frequent Portuguese port of call, where Mass was presumably often celebrated. Portuguese Zambesi missions never reached the Cape, and under Dutch governors from van Riebeek's arrival in 1652 public Catholic profession was forbidden. The first English governor reversed those measures, and later history the entry continues.

It stands as a researcher's dossier on the best-documented false-flag plan of the Cold War, documented in the government's own files.

govdocs-archive_org-thern-mythology-vol-:
Benjamin Thorpe published Northern Mythology in 1851, gathering the popular traditions and superstitions of Scandinavia and North Germany into three volumes. Volume I includes the Grottasöngr, the old song of the magic mill that ground out gold and then war.

Thorpe collected tales, charms, and customs from the people who still told and practiced them, then set them beside the old myths they descended from. His method helped make folklore a field a reader could hold in one book. The work became a classic of folklore studies, and its first volume remains a rich store of northern legend, belief, and story for any student of the North.
letters-from-the-cape:
Lucie Duff Gordon's Letters from the Cape were reissued by Oxford University Press in 1921. An editor's foreword says they are less familiar than Lady Anne Barnard's letters. Their first life was brief and partly hidden.

The letters first appeared in Galton's Vacation Tourists, third series, in 1864. Their simplicity and candor won brief public esteem there. Then the miscellany was forgotten, and the letters sank with it. Duff Gordon writes of South Africa with the same open eye she brought to Egypt. This reissue rescued a sharp, kind travel record. Her South African stay came before the Egyptian years. The same independence of mind marks both famous letter collections.
letters-to-sir-william-windham-and-mr-po:
Henry St. John, Viscount Bolingbroke, wrote these letters to Windham and Pope. Cassell published the volume in London, Paris, and Melbourne in 1894. An introduction traces Bolingbroke's life from his birth in 1678.

He was born at the family manor of Battersea, then a country village. His grandfather Sir Walter lived there with Cromwell's chief justice's daughter. Bolingbroke rose to lead Queen Anne's government, then fled into exile. His letters mix politics, philosophy, and friendship with Pope. They preserve a brilliant, fallen statesman's private voice. Pope, the poet, was Bolingbroke's close friend and ally. Their letters mix verse talk with high political memory.
lives-of-the-english-poets-prior-congrev:

Johnson replied that nothing in Prior excites to lewdness. Prior, he insisted, is a lady's book for any library. He praised Congreve's wit while condemning his plays' morals. Blackmore's religious purpose raised Johnson's estimate of his Creation poem. Lord Hailes censured Prior's tales as an eternal opprobrium. love-affairs-of-the-courts-of-europe:
Love Affairs of the Courts of Europe is a popular history by Thornton Hall. Hall was a barrister and a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries. His chapters roam the royal courts of Europe across past centuries. Titles promise a comedy queen, the Bonnie Prince's bride, and a peasant who won an empress.

Readers meet Richelieu the rake, the Sun King and a widow, and Bianca of Tuscany. A friend of Marie Antoinette appears, as do rival sisters and a mistress of intrigue. Hall tells these tales for pleasure, not for the classroom. Each chapter is a short, juicy court romance from real history. Together they show how love and power mixed at court.
medieval-europe:

nasa-tm-19660009115-loss-process-for-hel:
S J Bauer at Goddard wrote this December 1964 paper on how helium ions vanish from the upper atmosphere. Ions are charged atoms, made when sunlight strikes the thin upper air. Helium ions do not last forever there. Some process removes them, and its rate shapes the layer's makeup. Bauer names that loss process as his whole subject.

The upper air's mix of ions affects radio signals that pass through it. It also affects how satellites read the region with their instruments. A clear loss rate makes models of the ionosphere more honest. Bauer's short paper belongs to the careful work that turned scattered rocket and satellite readings into a coherent picture of the charged upper air.
nasa-tm-19690016179-the-global-structure:

Higher up, the protonosphere's daily swing and its nightside pattern across latitudes are mapped. nasa-tm-19710002046-effect-of-interactin:

Helium was shot at sonic speed into three kinds of flow. One held a pair of counter-rotating vortices, one a single vortex, and one no vortex at all. Injectors with swept edges made the swirls. nasa-tm-19710029182-retention-and-applic:
W. David Brown and Nancy Milly wrote this report for Marshall's Quality and Reliability Assurance Laboratory. It was revised on September 14, 1971, and issued as NASA TM X-64574. As the Saturn rocket program wound down, NASA risked losing hard-won engineering lessons. The report addresses how to keep that experience and apply it to future programs.

Its bulk is organized as working indexes. A hardware index sorts lessons by equipment, from amplifiers, batteries, and cables to computers, connectors, and power supplies. A problem index sorts them by cause, covering design, human error, maintenance, manufacturing, and procedures. Condition indexes and graphs let engineers find past failures by symptom. nasa-tm-19720003184-the-solar-envelope:
F Burlaga of NASA wrote this October 1971 study, NASA TM X-65739, on the region he calls the solar envelope. The envelope spans from about two to twenty five solar radii out from the Sun. Inside it, the solar wind changes character as it streams outward. Burlaga asked how those changes shape the wind later measured near Earth. The report runs to about fifty pages.

Within the envelope, the wind speed passes two key thresholds. It becomes supersonic, then faster than magnetic waves can travel. Magnetic energy in the flow also evolves across this zone. By the time the wind reaches Earth's distance, those early changes are built in. The study links near Sun physics to spacecraft readings taken far away.
nasa-tm-19720016238-analytic-short-perio:

Fisher's aim was a fast analytic theory, giving formulas rather than slow step-by-step computation.

He generalizes Kozai's short-period luni-solar theory so it works for any tilt of the ecliptic and any tilt of the Moon's orbit. Analytic first-order lunar perturbations to the orbital elements are derived in the analysis. A worked section applies the theory to the semi-major axis of the Intelsat 3F3 satellite.
